strengths: Soundness: The manuscript gives self-contained derivations for two concrete theoretical results. Theorem 3.1 connects the proposed jump-cost objective to an endpoint coupling cost for convex-interpolant conditional flows, yielding Hamming and embedding-distance special cases. Theorem 4.1 derives a path-space KL upper bound and specializes it to the computable perplexity bound in Equation (24).

Originality: Applying minibatch optimal-transport couplings to discrete flow matching and explicitly relating transition costs to endpoint token similarities is a potentially useful perspective. The perplexity-bound specialization also addresses a genuine evaluation difficulty for discrete flows.

Presentation: The paper is organized logically, supplies proofs in the appendix, and generally makes the intended relationship among discrete flows, transport couplings, and likelihood evaluation understandable.
Significance: If validated, the proposed coupling could reduce unnecessary token transitions, while the bound could provide a common evaluation quantity for discrete-flow language models.

Ethics and limitations: The work is theoretical and presents no immediate material ethical concern. Section 5 appropriately identifies the additional compute required by chains of flows and clearly labels that idea as future work.
weaknesses: The central practical claims are unsupported by evidence. There are no experiments, simulations, or even finite-state toy examples showing that minibatch OT reduces generation steps, improves model quality, remains stable with learned embeddings, or that the proposed perplexity bound is sufficiently tight to compare models. The conclusion nevertheless states that the method enables such evaluation and effective modeling.

Theorem 3.1 is described as an analogue of Benamou–Brenier and as an “equivalent Kantorovich formulation,” but the proof establishes an identity only for the particular factorized convex-interpolant flow induced by a fixed coupling. It does not establish equivalence between minimization over a general class of admissible discrete dynamics and Kantorovich optimization. This substantially narrows both the soundness and originality of the claimed OT interpretation.

The perplexity result lacks important regularity conditions. The rates contain dot(kappa_t)/(1-kappa_t) and can diverge as t approaches 1; the paper does not state assumptions ensuring finite integrals or cancellation. It also omits support/absolute-continuity conditions needed when the learned rate v is zero where w is positive, in which case the logarithmic term is infinite.

No analysis or empirical measurement of bound tightness is provided. An upper bound may be arbitrarily loose, and therefore does not by itself support the claim that it enables meaningful performance comparison. Numerical integration near the singular endpoint and estimator variance are also unaddressed.

The proposed method is underspecified for reproduction: there is no complete training algorithm or pseudocode, minibatch assignment procedure, embedding normalization or moving-average specification, numerical estimator for Equation (24), complexity analysis, implementation, or code. The source-distribution and flow-chain proposals are only sketches.

Several technical and notational problems reduce confidence. Equation (13) appears to train on x_0 although the surrounding derivation requires predicting x_1; the discrete-flow update in Section 2.3.1 appears to omit the timestep factor; N and L are used inconsistently; “similarity metric” is used for a dissimilarity cost; and Corollary 3.3 alternates between an L2 norm and its square.

The learned-embedding cost creates a coupled, nonstationary optimization problem. The manuscript mentions this under “Training Stability” but supplies neither a convergence argument nor evidence that the proposed moving-average heuristic prevents degenerate or unstable couplings.

The contribution’s significance is difficult to establish without comparisons against independent coupling, Hamming coupling, existing minibatch-OT flow matching, or established discrete-diffusion likelihood bounds. The mathematical results appear relatively direct specializations of conditional-flow and Markov jump-process identities.

The limitations discussion is incomplete. It does not address minibatch-OT bias and batch-size dependence, assignment cost for long sequences, dependence on embedding geometry, the restricted interpolant family, endpoint singularities, or looseness of the perplexity bound. There is also no explicit broader-impact or responsible-use discussion, although the absence is not itself a major ethical concern here.

strengths: The manuscript presents two identifiable theoretical ideas: an endpoint-cost identity for convex-interpolant discrete flows and a path-space KL bound specialized into a perplexity bound.
Theorem 3.1 has a reasonably transparent derivation, and the Hamming and embedding-distance cases provide useful intuition for constructing couplings that favor fewer or less severe token changes.
The paper is compact, readable, visually clean, and includes proofs in the appendix.
The questions addressed—reducing transitions during discrete generation and evaluating likelihood or perplexity—are practically relevant.
weaknesses: Soundness and evidence: there are no experiments. The paper never trains the proposed model, evaluates the perplexity bound, or measures transition count, generation quality, bound tightness, runtime, or stability. Claims that the approach reduces transitions or enables useful model comparison are therefore unsupported.

Theorem 3.1 is narrower than the Benamou–Brenier analogy suggests. For a fixed factorized convex interpolant, the proof reduces integrated conditional jump cost to expected endpoint cost under a chosen coupling; it does not establish a general dynamic/static OT equivalence over admissible discrete flows or show that minibatch OT improves a learned marginal flow.

The embedding cost changes during training. The paper only speculates about moving-average or decoupled embeddings, without defining a stable objective, providing convergence analysis, or empirically studying degeneracy and instability. Moreover, s is called a similarity metric although it functions as a dissimilarity cost.

The perplexity result is insufficiently qualified. Necessary support or absolute-continuity conditions for finite log ratios are not stated; the singular factor κ̇/(1−κ) near t=1 is not analyzed; and no numerical estimator, variance analysis, or evidence of bound tightness is provided. Thus, practical computability and usefulness are not established.

Presentation contains consequential notation problems: Eq. 13 appears to train p_{1|t} on x_0 rather than target x_1; Eq. 21 uses −log p_t(x_1;θ) where p_1 is required; N and L are inconsistent; rates are called probabilities; and L2 versus squared-L2 terminology is imprecise.

Originality appears limited because the results closely specialize existing discrete flow matching, minibatch OT, and Markov-jump path-KL constructions. The paper does not clearly separate genuinely new theory from direct algebraic specialization.

Reproducibility is inadequate: there is no algorithm or pseudocode, model or dataset specification, training setup, numerical integration method, hyperparameters, code, or artifact. The source-distribution and chained-flow proposals remain conceptual sketches.

The limitations discussion is incomplete. It does not adequately address the narrow interpolant assumption, minibatch bias, learned-cost degeneracy, computational scaling, or potentially loose perplexity bounds. No acute ethical issue is evident, but without experiments the work also cannot assess language-model memorization, bias, or misuse. Overall, the paper has discernible ideas, but major evidential, technical, and reproducibility gaps prevent acceptance.

strengths: The paper targets two genuine obstacles in discrete flow matching: choosing couplings that favor simpler categorical trajectories and evaluating models when exact likelihoods are unavailable.

Theorem 3.1 provides a clean endpoint-cost identity for convex-interpolant conditional flows. Its Hamming and squared embedding-distance specializations give an intuitive connection between transition minimization and minibatch optimal transport.

The path-space KL argument underlying Theorem 4.1 is potentially useful. Specializing it to the discrete-flow parameterization produces an explicit perplexity upper bound rather than relying only on sample-quality metrics.

The manuscript is generally well organized, and the appendices provide substantive derivations rather than merely asserting the main theoretical results. It also candidly notes training-instability and computational concerns surrounding adaptive embeddings and chains of flows.
The work raises no evident research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: There are no experiments. Consequently, the central practical claims—that minibatch OT reduces transitions or sampling steps, improves modeling quality, and that the proposed perplexity bound enables meaningful model comparison—receive no empirical support. Even small controlled categorical experiments measuring trajectory cost, generation quality, and bound tightness are needed.

The perplexity bound is called computable but is not operationally validated. The paper gives no Monte Carlo estimator, variance or discretization analysis, numerical-stability treatment, or comparison against exact likelihood on a tractable problem. The factor dot(kappa_t)/(1-kappa_t) can be singular near t=1, so the bound may be infinite or numerically unusable unless additional endpoint behavior is established.

Theorem 4.1 omits important technical conditions, including rate regularity and integrability and the support/absolute-continuity requirement that v_t be positive wherever w_t is positive. Without these conditions, the logarithmic rate ratio may be undefined and the stated bound need not be finite.

The minibatch-OT method is underspecified for reproducibility: there is no algorithm or pseudocode, coupling solver, batch-size analysis, computational complexity, cost normalization, or resolved policy for updating the learned embeddings used in the transport cost. The proposed source distributions are likewise not evaluated.

Several proposed elements are preliminary rather than completed contributions. In particular, chains of discrete flows are listed among the contributions but appear only as untested future work, while the embedding-stability discussion offers possible strategies without analysis or evidence.

The theoretical novelty is meaningful but limited: Theorem 3.1 is an elementary identity restricted to a particular convex interpolant, and Theorem 4.1 specializes a standard continuous-time Markov-chain path-KL result. The manuscript does not establish tightness, improved sample complexity, or generation-speed consequences.

Notation and presentation contain correctness-affecting inconsistencies: the transition update in Section 2.3.1 appears to omit the step-size factor; Equation 13 uses the source token x_0 where the surrounding derivation suggests the target x_1; Equation 21 switches between p_t and p_1; and the text repeatedly calls a nonnegative dissimilarity cost a similarity metric. Theorem 3.1 also implicitly needs symmetry to exchange s(x_0,x_1) with the proof's s(x_1,x_0). These should be corrected before others build on the results.

strengths: Soundness: The paper gives substantial derivations for the dynamic/static transport identity and two perplexity upper bounds. The pointwise equality for per-position convex interpolants supports using minibatch coupling with Hamming or embedding-based costs, and the appendices expose the proof steps rather than treating the results as black boxes.

Significance: Reducing sampling steps for discrete flow language models is practically important. On the OpenWebText experiment, OT consistently improves the GPT-2-judged generative perplexity of the bag-of-words model, and the reported OT overhead is modest.

Evaluation breadth: The paper includes a GPT-2-sized experiment, 10,240 generated samples, two evaluator models, transport-cost measurements, solver and batch-size ablations, entropy measurements, and small controlled experiments that directly count transitions.

Originality: Combining minibatch OT with discrete flow matching, introducing the multimask source, and adapting path-space KL bounds to general DFM constitute a coherent contribution, even though each component is closely related to existing flow-matching or discrete-diffusion ideas.

Presentation: The main narrative is generally understandable, and the extensive appendices provide algorithms, architecture and optimization settings, proofs, additional tables, and generated examples.
weaknesses: Soundness and framing: The advertised categorical Benamou-Brenier result is considerably narrower than the name suggests. For the prescribed convex-interpolant conditional flow, the dynamics are already determined by the coupling, and the proof reduces the expected weighted jump rate to the endpoint cost for each coupling. The paper itself acknowledges that taking an infimum is “purely formal.” It does not establish an equivalence after optimizing over a broad class of discrete dynamics, so the conceptual advance is more modest than the headline framing.

The central “8-fold” result rests on evaluator-model perplexity rather than likelihood or a comprehensive quality/diversity assessment. With GPT-2 Large, DFM-B-OT at 128 steps and DFM-B at 1024 steps score 185.54 and 185.83 in Appendix Table 10, a difference smaller than the reported sample-level standard deviations. With Llama 3.1, the corresponding values are 225.36 and 223.77, so the claimed match is evaluator-dependent. Unigram-like entropy alone does not exclude repetition, generic text, memorization, or higher-order mode loss.

The uncertainty estimates are over generated samples, while no independent training runs or variation across random seeds are reported. Consequently, the work does not establish that the relatively small OT gains are robust to training variance.

The multimask comparison is materially confounded. DFM-MMLM introduces 50,257 distinct, unrestricted mask embeddings; at width 768 this is roughly 38.6 million additional embedding parameters. The paper nevertheless describes the architecture as only about 5% larger than GPT-2 and provides no parameter-matched baseline or ablation over the number of masks. Its improvement over ordinary masked flow therefore cannot confidently be attributed to the proposed source distribution.

The embedding-based OT cost uses learnable model embeddings, so its scale and geometry change during training and admit potentially degenerate representations. The authors mention this interaction only as future work; they do not report normalization, stop-gradient behavior, a frozen semantic metric, embedding-scale diagnostics, or an ablation establishing that the learned transport cost remains meaningful.

The evidence for the perplexity bounds as useful training objectives is mixed. DFM-S, which uses the actual bound, is substantially worse in generative perplexity than DFM-O. DFM-N removes the singular weighting by multiplying by (1-t), so it is no longer the stated bound, and it is slightly worse than ordinary cross-entropy DFM-O at 1024 steps. Tightness is evaluated only in tiny hand-constructed examples, while the paper concedes that it cannot be assessed in the realistic setting.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or checkpoint availability is stated; seeds and run counts are absent; the main embedding-cost Sinkhorn regularization and several coupling details are unspecified; and the entropy metric and evaluator-perplexity protocol are not defined precisely enough to reconstruct. Testing OT-trained bounds also requires a heuristic minibatch reconstruction of an inaccessible coupling.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies. Main Table 3 and Appendix Table 10 report different values for the same DFM-B and DFM-B-OT experiments—for example, 192.75 versus 191.48 at 128 steps and 185.12 versus 185.83 at 1024 steps. There are also smaller textual/table discrepancies such as 74.84 versus 74.87 jumps and numerous typographical errors.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The limitations section discusses only coupling/embedding co-adaptation and omits the surrogate-evaluation limitation, parameter confound, absence of multi-run evidence, and restriction to one training corpus and model scale. The generated-sample warning and LLM-use statement are welcome, but the paper does not discuss OpenWebText licensing/provenance, memorization and privacy, representational harms, or compute/environmental costs. These are not fatal ethical violations, but treatment is inadequate for a language-generation study.

strengths: The central jump-cost identity is plausible and explicitly derived for convex per-position interpolants.
The paper combines theory with GPT-2-scale OpenWebText experiments and reports results across multiple sampling budgets.
Evaluation uses both GPT-2-Large and Llama-3.1-8B judges and includes computational-overhead measurements.
The authors acknowledge that OT-model bound evaluation relies on an approximate implicit coupling.
weaknesses: Soundness: The headline 8-fold acceleration applies only to the weak bag-of-words DFM-B baseline. For the strongest multimask model, OT provides only small gains, with mixed or nearly tied Llama results at several step counts.

Soundness: The multimask comparison is confounded by 50,257 additional learned mask tokens. The manuscript neither reports model-specific parameter counts nor provides a parameter-matched control, and its stated vocabulary sizes are inconsistent.

Soundness: The path-KL theorems omit necessary regularity and support assumptions, and their continuous-time limit arguments are informal. The reported OpenWebText schedule also has k_0=0.001, violating the stated k_0=0 endpoint condition without justification that the bounds remain valid.

The derived masked-flow bound, DFM-S, is not the best objective. The preferred DFM-N multiplies it by 1-t and is no longer the claimed bound. Tightness is examined only in tiny constructed examples, while OT-model bound estimates are explicitly heuristic.

Originality/significance: Theorem 3.1 is an identity for a restricted flow already determined by its coupling; optimization over flows is merely formal. The likelihood results substantially extend existing diffusion/path-KL bounds, while a similar concurrent DFM result is acknowledged.

Empirical rigor: Apparently only one training run is used per setting. Reported deviations do not establish training-seed robustness, token entropy alone is inadequate evidence that diversity is preserved, and important parameter-matched and semantic-cost controls are absent.

Reproducibility/presentation: No code release is identified. Missing or inconsistent details include parameter counts, large-scale Sinkhorn regularization, gradient handling for learned cost embeddings, seeds, sampling details, and Monte Carlo estimation procedures. Proposition 4.4 also appears without a required time integral in the main text.

Limitations/ethics: The limitations section omits the central comparison and evaluation weaknesses and does not discuss privacy, copyright, bias, toxicity, or misuse considerations associated with OpenWebText language generation.

strengths: Soundness: The paper develops a coherent theoretical story. Theorem 3.1 proves an exact equality between the proposed weighted-jump dynamic objective and a Kantorovich cost for per-position convex-interpolant flows, and the appendix supplies a detailed derivation. The two perplexity upper bounds are also derived from path-space KL arguments and connected to established discrete-diffusion objectives, including MD4 as a special case.

Empirical support: The experiments cover a useful progression from controlled Shakespeare settings to GPT-2-scale OpenWebText training. The headline efficiency result is supported by Table 3: DFM-B-OT at 128 sampling steps attains approximately the same GPT-2-Large generative perplexity as DFM-B at 1024 steps. Results with a second evaluator, transport-cost measurements, solver and minibatch-size ablations, and entropy measurements provide additional corroboration.

Significance: Reducing the sampling cost of discrete flow models is practically important. The likelihood bounds also give DFM models a principled intrinsic evaluation tool and permit comparisons with autoregressive and discrete-diffusion models where exact likelihood is unavailable.

Originality: The weighted-jump formulation, its coupling-level characterization for convex interpolants, and the multi-mask construction form a novel and conceptually well-integrated contribution. Multi-mask flows cleverly preserve time-independent predictive probabilities while providing a nontrivial source distribution on which OT can operate.

Presentation: The main narrative is generally clear, and the manuscript explicitly distinguishes generative perplexity, perplexity upper bounds, and exact likelihood. The extensive appendix contains proofs, algorithms, architecture and optimizer details, ablations, bound-tightness examples, and generated samples.
Research ethics: No major ethical concern is apparent. The paper discloses LLM-assisted editing and warns that uncurated generated text may contain inaccuracies or culturally sensitive material.
weaknesses: Soundness/general scope: Theorem 3.1 is exact only for the restricted family of per-position convex interpolants whose dynamics are already determined by the coupling. It is therefore not a general discrete Benamou-Brenier theorem over arbitrary admissible flows, and the paper's terminology occasionally makes the result sound broader than it is.

The likelihood bounds lack fully stated regularity and support assumptions needed when rates or learned probabilities vanish and logarithmic rate ratios occur. Moreover, the experimental schedule k_t=0.001+(1-0.001)t does not satisfy the stated theoretical endpoint condition k_0=0; the manuscript should explain this truncation or approximation and its effect on the bounds.

The strongest empirical gains are not established across independent training seeds. Reported deviations appear to quantify evaluation-sample variability, not run-to-run uncertainty, which is especially important for the relatively small improvements of multi-mask OT over multi-mask alone.

The claim that quality is preserved is based mainly on perplexity under GPT-2-Large and Llama-3.1-8B evaluators. These are useful proxies but not direct assessments of coherence or factuality, and no human evaluation or broader text-quality benchmark is included. Likewise, the assertion that diversity is preserved relies on an insufficiently explained entropy statistic.

The paper's use of “perplexity” requires care: many values are upper bounds, while the main sampling-efficiency values are evaluator-model perplexities rather than likelihood perplexities of the proposed model. Bound tightness is examined only in tiny constructed examples, and the appendix concedes that bound evaluation for OT-trained models uses a heuristic minibatch approximation because the implicit coupling is inaccessible.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Although architecture, optimizer, batch size, training duration, and hardware are reported, the manuscript does not provide code or sufficiently specify all OT and sampling details, such as the main Sinkhorn regularization, embedding-distance normalization, random seeds, preprocessing, evaluator scoring protocol, and exact entropy calculation.

There are small but visible reporting inconsistencies: several DFM-B and DFM-B-OT numbers in main-text Table 3 differ from the corresponding values in Appendix Table 10. The statement that the squared embedding cost is an “L2 norm” is also imprecise—it is the squared Euclidean norm of the concatenated sequence embedding.

The limitations section is too narrow. It discusses coupling/embedding co-adaptation but omits the single-scale evaluation, evaluator dependence, lack of training-seed replication, heuristic OT-bound evaluation, substantial training compute, and biases or licensing considerations associated with OpenWebText. These issues limit confidence but do not negate the paper's useful contribution.
